messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Terrorism
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform, Military Topics: Talks about military, Auditory/Threat: Gunshot noise
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Carry Weapon: carry weapon, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rafael Méndez is a 70-year-old widowed dentist who had practiced for decades in the same community, a man who had always taken pride in steady hands and a calming voice. The event he returns to only in fragments happened two years ago, when he was leaving his office at dusk after a late patient. A nearby explosion was followed by gunfire in the street, and in the confusion he found himself pressed against the wall of his own building, hearing sharp cracks ricochet between storefronts while armed uniformed responders flooded the block. What stayed with him was not a tidy story but a rush of sensory pieces: the concussive pop of shots, the metallic smell in the air, the sight of men in uniform shouting commands he could not fully process, and the certainty that he could be killed before he understood what was happening. Even now, when he tries to explain it, he falters. He says the memory does not come back as a narrative so much as “all at once,” and when it does he is overcome so quickly that he has to stop talking.

In the months afterward, specific cues in daily life began to carry the force of the attack. At the dental office, when a police officer came in uniform to ask for directions in the building, Rafael felt his chest lock and his attention narrow; conversations about military operations in the waiting room had a similar effect, as did the crack of a dropped instrument tray or any noise resembling a gunshot. Those moments did not stay mild. The sight of a uniform or talk about the military could pull the event back with such sensory immediacy that he was briefly back against that wall, hearing shots and feeling the same helpless terror, and the sheer overwhelm pushed him to cut things off however he could. He began turning off the television whenever news coverage mentioned bombings or armed attacks, and if patients started discussing military conflicts, he found reasons to leave the room. He also replayed the event afterward in a punishing way, repeatedly blaming himself for having stayed late, for not leaving earlier, for not somehow having known what was about to happen.

His fear increasingly organized itself around the possibility of danger being everywhere. Loud or unexpected sounds made him jolt into immediate alertness, and he started watching people closely for signs that they might harm him. Entering any room, whether it was a restaurant, church, or his own clinic, he would first locate the exits before he could settle. At work this had become almost automatic: before greeting the next patient, Rafael would scan the operatory door, the hallway, and the back exit, and if he heard a sharp noise from the sterilization area, his mind went at once to attack. That constant sense of threat fed directly into what he did to cope. He obtained a weapon and began carrying it, telling himself he would never again be defenseless. He kept avoiding televised news, and after episodes of alarm he would sit alone and revisit his mistakes, as if relentless self-blame might somehow prepare him for the next time.

Those strategies have not brought relief. Carrying the weapon has made him more preoccupied with who around him might be dangerous, and scanning for exits has made uniforms, military talk, and sudden noises harder to ignore, not easier. Avoiding news has narrowed his world while leaving him more reactive when he unexpectedly overhears military topics in public, because he has given himself so little chance to encounter any reminder without bracing for catastrophe. The rumination is especially corrosive: after he spends an evening circling what he “should have done,” the memory feels even less speakable and more like a sensory assault, so vivid and overwhelming that he has to shut down when it surfaces. In turn, because the memory remains so unprocessed and wordless, the next trigger lands with full force. A loud bang in the office parking lot, a veteran in uniform in the elevator, a waiting-room television mentioning troops overseas—each is enough to make the old danger feel present again.

Over time this has changed how he works and lives. Staff have noticed that Rafael is slower to move between patients because he pauses at doorways and checks the hall. He schedules fewer late appointments and avoids staff lunches where the television might be on. As a widower, he already spent much of his time alone, and now the isolation has deepened; there is no one at home to interrupt the hours he spends going over the event and condemning himself. He finally sought help after a recent incident in his clinic when a sudden crashing noise sent him reaching toward the weapon he carries, leaving him shaken and ashamed in front of an assistant. What frightens him most is the sense that he is still living inside that moment, vulnerable to any uniform, any military conversation, any sharp sound. What he hopes, though he says it cautiously, is that he might learn how to remember what happened without being pulled all the way back into it.
